summary.text: Heracles, mightiest of the heroes, was born to Alcmene at Thebes, who lay in the arms of great Zeus and bore him.
summary.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 943–944; Homer, Odyssey 11.266–268; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.8

summary.text: Of Perseid blood through both his mother Alcmene and the house of Amphitryon, he was conceived in a contested night: Zeus, in the likeness of her husband, lay with Alcmene, so that the elder twin was reckoned the son of the god while Amphitryon remained his mortal father — and so his paternity was forever divided between them.

story.text: His descent runs back to Perseus and Andromeda, who had five sons in Mycenae — Alcaeus, Sthenelus, Heleus, Mestor, and Electryon — and a daughter, Gorgophone. Alcaeus begot Amphitryon, and Electryon a daughter, Alcmene; so the houses that would meet in Heracles were both branches of the one Perseid stock.

Before Amphitryon reached Thebes, Zeus came by night, prolonged the one night threefold, took on Amphitryon's likeness, and bedded with Alcmene. She bore two sons: Heracles, whom she had by Zeus and who was the elder by one night, and Iphicles, whom she had by Amphitryon — a double union that left his fatherhood disputed between the god and the man.

When the child was eight months old, Hera, desiring his destruction, sent two huge serpents to the bed. Alcmene called Amphitryon to help, but the infant Heracles rose up and killed the serpents, strangling them with both his hands. Pherecydes, however, says it was Amphitryon who laid the serpents in the bed, to learn which of the two boys was his own.

Hera's enmity reached back even to his birth. On the day Alcmene was to bring forth Heracles in fair-crowned Thebe, Zeus boasted that a child of his blood would that day be born to rule over all his neighbours; Hera bound him by oath, then hastened the birth of Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus and likewise of the Perseid line, in the seventh month, and held back Alcmene's labour — so the rule fell to Eurystheus, and Heracles was made his subject.
He was not always called Heracles. When he came in time to Delphi and asked the god where he should dwell, the Pythian priestess then first named him Heracles; before that he had been called Alcides.
